title: Wall Street Plunges Into Correction as AI Rout Deepens
content: US stocks suffered a brutal sell-off on Friday, with the S&P 500 sliding 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow falling 1.93% (949.73 points) to 48,147.33, both ending more than 10% below recent highs and confirming a market correction. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.28% to 22,617.73, wiping out its 2026 gains and turning negative for the year, as mounting doubts over how the AI build-out is being financed combined with a slump in Nvidia to drive the heaviest selling since the spring. On a weekly basis the Nasdaq shed roughly 10% and the S&P around 8.6%, its worst week in more than 18 months.
summary: The S&P 500 and Dow fell into correction and the Nasdaq erased its 2026 gains as an AI-driven sell-off accelerated on Friday.
context:
• US equities had already endured a bruising autumn as investors questioned whether vast AI infrastructure spending will pay off and whether megacap valuations were stretched.

• Market leadership has been unusually concentrated in a handful of AI winners, leaving indices acutely exposed when sentiment on the trade turns.

• A hawkish repricing of Fed policy, with a December rate rise now widely expected, has lifted real yields and sapped appetite for richly valued growth shares.
happened:
• The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow lost 1.93% to 48,147.33 on Friday, both closing more than 10% below their recent peaks.

• The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73, erasing its gains for 2026, while the Nasdaq-100 briefly entered a bear market on an intraday basis.

• For the week the Dow fell about 8%, the S&P roughly 8.6% and the Nasdaq Composite around 10%, marking the broad market's steepest weekly loss in more than 18 months.
implications:
• A confirmed correction raises the risk of further forced and systematic selling as momentum and volatility-targeting strategies cut exposure.

• With the AI-financing narrative now in focus, any sign of slowing data-centre spend or tighter credit could extend the drawdown.

• A hawkish Fed path into December leaves little monetary cushion should the sell-off feed through to the real economy.
importance:
• Corrections in both the S&P 500 and Dow signal that the risk-off move has broadened well beyond a narrow group of AI names.

• The speed of the Nasdaq's reversal underlines how crowded and leveraged the AI trade had become.

• Positioning into year-end now hinges on whether dip-buyers return or whether the unwind has further to run.

title: Nikkei Sheds 5% as AI Sell-Off Rattles Asia
content: Asian equities were hammered on Friday as the global retreat from artificial-intelligence and chip stocks swept through the region, with Japan's Nikkei 225 plunging more than 3,000 points, or about 5.1%, to close at 56,436.65. South Korea's Kospi fell 5.2% to 4,869.12 and Taiwan's benchmark dropped more than 6%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 2.2% to 22,333.88 and the Shanghai Composite eased 1.3% to 3,532.10. The rout marked a sharp reversal after the Nikkei had closed higher only a day earlier, underscoring how quickly sentiment towards the AI trade soured across markets.
summary: Japan's Nikkei fell about 5.1% and South Korea's Kospi 5.2% as the global AI and chip sell-off swept through Asian markets.
context:
• Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese indices are heavily weighted towards semiconductor and AI-supply-chain names, amplifying losses when the global tech trade unwinds.

• Asian markets had rallied strongly through 2026 on AI optimism, leaving them exposed once doubts over the build-out's financing took hold.

• A firmer US dollar and rising global yields have added pressure on regional equities and currencies alike.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 shed more than 3,000 points to finish at 56,436.65, down about 5.1%, a day after closing higher near 59,444.

• The Kospi dropped 5.2% to 4,869.12 and Taiwan's benchmark fell more than 6%, among the hardest-hit in the region.

• Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 2.2% to 22,333.88 and the Shanghai Composite slipped 1.3% to 3,532.10.
implications:
• Heavy losses in chip-heavy markets could prompt further de-risking by global funds with large Asian technology exposure.

• Sustained weakness in regional currencies may complicate policy for central banks already wary of imported inflation.

• A deeper or more prolonged AI drawdown would test earnings assumptions across Asia's export-driven semiconductor supply chain.
importance:
• Asia's chipmakers sit at the heart of the global AI hardware chain, so sharp falls there reverberate through world markets.

• The scale of the Nikkei's one-day drop signals that the sell-off is global rather than confined to US megacaps.

• Regional benchmarks are now a key barometer of whether the AI correction is stabilising or spreading.

title: European Shares Cap Worst Week Since March
content: European equities tumbled on Friday to round off their steepest weekly fall since March, as investors continued to unwind AI-linked bets and chip names led the declines. The pan-European STOXX 600 lost about 5.8% over the week, with Germany's DAX closing Friday down 2.6% at 24,802.78 and France's CAC 40 off 1.9% at 7,927.75, dragged lower by heavy falls in semiconductor-exposed shares such as ASML and Infineon. London's FTSE 100 proved more resilient, slipping just 1% to 10,346.34 as stronger-than-expected UK retail sales offered some cushion.
summary: The STOXX 600 fell about 5.8% on the week, its worst since March, as chip stocks led a broad European retreat.
context:
• European indices have tracked the global AI trade closely, leaving them vulnerable as sentiment towards the sector deteriorated.

• Semiconductor-equipment and chip names such as ASML and Infineon carry outsized index weight, concentrating the damage.

• The UK has shown pockets of domestic resilience, with firmer consumer data helping the FTSE 100 outperform continental peers.
happened:
• The DAX closed Friday down 2.6% at 24,802.78 and the CAC 40 fell 1.9% to 7,927.75, a fourth straight session of losses.

• The STOXX 600 lost roughly 5.8% over the week, its worst weekly performance since March, with ASML and Infineon among the biggest fallers.

• The FTSE 100 held up better, down about 1% at 10,346.34, supported by stronger-than-expected UK retail sales.
implications:
• Continued outflows from European chip names could weigh on indices that rely heavily on a small cluster of technology stocks.

• Relative FTSE resilience may draw defensive flows if the AI-led sell-off persists.

• A sustained risk-off move could tighten European financial conditions just as growth remains fragile.
importance:
• The worst week since March signals that the AI unwind is a cross-regional event, not a US-only story.

• Europe's heavy exposure to semiconductor-equipment makers leaves its benchmarks sensitive to every twist in the chip cycle.

• Divergence between the FTSE and continental indices highlights where defensive investors may seek shelter.

title: Markets Lock In December Fed Hike as Yields Whipsaw
content: Investors moved to price a near-certain US interest-rate increase at the Federal Reserve's 9 December meeting, cementing a remarkable shift from the rate cuts expected only weeks ago as inflation runs hot. Front-end Treasuries swung sharply through the week: two-year yields fell about 20 basis points, their steepest weekly decline since August 2025, as the equity rout drove haven demand, while the 10-year note ended around 4.95% after touching 5.14% the previous week. The Fed's target range stands at 3.75%–4.00% following October's hold, and traders are now even debating whether policymakers could opt for a larger half-point move.
summary: Markets priced a near-certain December Fed hike as Treasury yields whipsawed, with two-year yields posting their steepest weekly fall since August 2025.
context:
• The Fed lifted rates once in 2026 and held in October at 3.75%–4.00%, but sticky inflation has flipped the market from pricing cuts to pricing hikes.

• A Reuters poll found every surveyed economist expects a December increase, reflecting an unusually firm consensus.

• Rising real yields have been a key driver of the pressure on richly valued equities and non-yielding assets.
happened:
• Markets moved to price a December rate rise as all but certain, with some traders weighing a larger-than-usual half-point move.

• Two-year Treasury yields fell roughly 20 basis points on the week, their biggest weekly drop since August 2025, as the equity sell-off spurred haven buying.

• The 10-year yield ended near 4.95%, down from about 5.14% the prior week, leaving the curve volatile into the December meeting.
implications:
• A hiking Fed would keep financial conditions tight, pressuring equity valuations and lifting borrowing costs across the economy.

• Haven flows into short-dated Treasuries could persist if the equity drawdown deepens, keeping the front end volatile.

• Any upside surprise in coming inflation data could revive debate over the pace and size of further hikes.
importance:
• Rate expectations anchor valuations across equities, credit, currencies and commodities, so the repricing reverberates everywhere.

• The pivot from cuts to hikes has upended the core assumption behind this year's risk rally.

• Sharp swings at the front end show how sensitive bond markets have become to each data point and Fed signal.

title: Gold Tumbles Towards $3,500 as Real Yields Climb
content: Gold fell sharply on Friday, sliding about 2.5% to around $3,513 an ounce and extending a steep retreat from the $4,100-plus levels seen only weeks earlier. The slump came as the 10-year real yield rose to about 2.88% and the dollar firmed on near-certain bets of a December Fed rate rise, raising the opportunity cost of holding the non-yielding metal. The move leaves bullion down sharply from its January peak and underlines how a hawkish rates backdrop has turned a former safe haven into one of the month's notable casualties.
summary: Gold fell about 2.5% to roughly $3,513 an ounce as rising real yields and a firmer dollar pressured the non-yielding metal.
context:
• Gold surged to record territory earlier in 2026 but has since reversed as real yields climbed and rate-cut bets evaporated.

• Bullion's appeal weakens when real yields rise, since the metal pays no income and competes with inflation-protected bonds.

• A stronger dollar, driven by hawkish Fed repricing, adds a further headwind for dollar-priced commodities.
happened:
• Spot gold fell about 2.5% on Friday to around $3,513 an ounce, near $3,500 and well below the $4,100-plus levels of early November.

• The 10-year real yield rose to roughly 2.88% and the dollar firmed as markets priced a likely December Fed hike.

• The decline leaves gold down sharply from its January high, among the weaker commodity performers of the month.
implications:
• Further increases in real yields would keep pressure on gold and other non-yielding assets.

• A sustained bullion sell-off could weigh on gold-mining equities and precious-metals funds.

• Should the equity rout intensify, haven demand could yet re-emerge and partially offset the rates drag.
importance:
• Gold's slide alongside equities shows how a hawkish rates regime can undercut traditional diversifiers.

• The metal's reversal from record highs is a reminder that real yields, not just risk sentiment, drive its price.

• Commodity weakness reinforces the broader message that tighter policy is reshaping cross-asset returns.

title: Dollar Firm as Yen Lingers Near 160 and Intervention Warnings Grow
content: The dollar held firm through the week on near-certain bets of a December Fed rate rise, keeping the Japanese yen pinned close to the 160-per-dollar level that has unsettled Tokyo. Japanese officials repeated warnings that they stand ready to respond to excessive currency moves, while the euro languished near multi-month lows against the greenback after earlier touching its weakest since April 2025. By Friday the dollar eased modestly against the yen as the global equity rout spurred some haven demand for the Japanese currency, though the broader trend of dollar strength remained intact.
summary: The dollar stayed firm on Fed-hike bets, keeping the yen near 160 and prompting fresh Japanese warnings over excessive currency moves.
context:
• Wide US-Japan rate differentials have pressured the yen throughout 2026, repeatedly testing levels that invite official scrutiny.

• A hawkish repricing of Fed policy has broadly lifted the dollar and weighed on the euro and other majors.

• Tokyo has a track record of verbal and, at times, direct intervention when yen weakness becomes disorderly.
happened:
• The yen hovered close to 160 per dollar as the greenback firmed on bets of a December Fed increase.

• Japanese officials warned they would respond to excessive moves, while the euro sat near multi-month lows after touching its weakest since April 2025.

• On Friday the dollar slipped modestly against the yen as the equity sell-off spurred some safe-haven demand for the currency.
implications:
• A further test of 160 could prompt Japanese intervention, injecting two-way volatility into the pair.

• Continued dollar strength would tighten global financial conditions and pressure emerging-market currencies.

• The euro's weakness may complicate the inflation outlook for the euro area via costlier imports.
importance:
• Dollar-yen is among the most closely watched gauges of global rate differentials and risk appetite.

• Intervention risk makes the pair a potential source of sudden cross-asset volatility.

• Currency moves feed directly into corporate earnings, trade balances and central-bank calculations.

title: Bitcoin Languishes Near $64,000 as Fed-Hike Bets Bite
content: Bitcoin remained under heavy pressure in the latest sessions, trading around $64,000 and roughly 21% below its level of a month earlier, as near-certain bets on a December Fed rate rise and sustained ETF outflows drained appetite for digital assets. The token has slipped beneath its 200-day moving average, a closely watched technical level, while the broader crypto complex has tracked the sell-off in high-beta technology shares. With risk appetite souring across global markets, the rout has reinforced how tightly digital assets remain tied to the fate of the AI-driven risk trade and the rates outlook.
summary: Bitcoin hovered near $64,000, down about 21% on the month, as Fed-hike bets and ETF outflows pressured digital assets.
context:
• Digital assets have traded in close sympathy with high-beta technology stocks through 2026, amplifying losses when risk appetite sours.

• Spot bitcoin ETFs have become a key marginal source of demand, so sustained outflows now weigh directly on prices.

• A hawkish repricing of Fed policy has lifted real yields and sapped appetite for non-yielding, speculative assets.
happened:
• Bitcoin traded around $64,000, roughly 21% below its level a month earlier, and slipped beneath its 200-day moving average.

• Mounting bets on a December Fed hike and continued spot-ETF redemptions weighed on sentiment.

• The broad crypto market tracked the wider retreat from AI and high-beta technology shares.
implications:
• Persistent ETF redemptions would remove a pillar of demand and leave the market more exposed to forced, leveraged selling.

• A firmer Fed path and higher real yields could keep pressure on speculative assets into the December meeting.

• A decisive break of key technical levels risks triggering a further cascade of liquidations.
importance:
• Bitcoin has become a real-time barometer of broad risk appetite, so its slide signals caution spreading across markets.

• ETF flows offer a transparent read on institutional positioning that traders now watch closely.

• The rout underlines how tightly digital assets are tied to the AI risk trade and the rates outlook.

title: Nvidia Slumps Despite Record Results in First Report Since Huang Exit
content: Nvidia shares slid sharply after the chipmaker's first quarterly report since the abrupt departure of long-time chief executive Jensen Huang, even though results comfortably beat expectations with earnings of $2.68 a share against a $2.49 consensus and record revenue. The stock fell about 3% the day after earnings and then tumbled around 13% on Friday amid reports of a US securities-regulator probe, leaving it down roughly 19% since early November and dragging on indices worldwide. The slide came as investors questioned the durability of AI demand and fretted over how the industry's vast infrastructure spending is being financed.
summary: Nvidia shares slumped after its first post-Huang earnings, falling about 13% on Friday despite record results, amid reports of a regulatory probe.
context:
• Nvidia sits at the centre of the global AI trade, so its share moves ripple through semiconductors, megacap tech and risk sentiment broadly.

• The report was the first since chief executive Jensen Huang resigned abruptly in mid-November, leaving a leadership vacuum the board is still filling.

• Investors were already questioning whether vast AI infrastructure spending will generate adequate returns.
happened:
• Nvidia posted earnings of $2.68 a share, beating the $2.49 consensus, alongside record revenue and a raised growth target.

• The stock still fell about 3% the day after results and then dropped roughly 13% on Friday amid reports of a US securities-regulator investigation.

• The decline left Nvidia down about 19% since early November, weighing heavily on US and global indices.
implications:
• A prolonged CEO search and regulatory uncertainty could keep a discount on the shares and across the wider chip complex.

• Continued weakness in the sector's bellwether risks deepening the broader AI-led market drawdown.

• Clarity on succession, the regulatory position and demand durability will be critical to stabilising sentiment.
importance:
• Nvidia's sheer index weight means its swings move the S&P 500 and Nasdaq directly.

• That a record beat failed to lift the stock crystallises how fragile confidence in the AI trade has become.

• The episode ties company-specific risk to the market-wide question of AI-spending sustainability.

title: Anthropic Pulls Off Record IPO Even as AI Stocks Crack
content: Anthropic, the artificial-intelligence company behind the Claude models, made its Nasdaq debut under the ticker 'ANT', pricing at $83 a share and raising about $81.3bn in what ranks as the largest initial public offering on record. The stock opened at $111.50, some 34% above the offer price, and touched an intraday high near $115 that valued the company above $2tn before paring gains to close its first session up about 17% at $97.17. The debut defied a broad sell-off in AI shares, though the stock then fell around 9% the following day as the wider tech rout intensified, remaining above its IPO price.
summary: Anthropic raised about $81.3bn in a record Nasdaq IPO, closing its first day up 17% at $97.17 before easing as AI stocks sold off.
context:
• The listing is the most prominent AI IPO yet and a major test of public-market appetite for the sector after a turbulent autumn.

• Anthropic had been expected to seek a landmark valuation, and the deal's scale makes it the largest IPO on record.

• The float priced into one of the sharpest AI-stock sell-offs of the year, heightening scrutiny of its reception.
happened:
• Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share and raised about $81.3bn through the sale of roughly 980 million Class A shares.

• The stock opened at $111.50, up about 34%, hit an intraday high near $115 valuing it above $2tn, and closed its first day up about 17% at $97.17.

• Shares then fell around 9% the next day as the broader AI sell-off deepened, but stayed above the IPO price.
implications:
• A debut above the offer price keeps the AI-IPO window ajar, but the subsequent drop signals fragile sentiment.

• The sheer scale of the raise could pull liquidity from other richly valued technology names.

• Ongoing questions over how AI infrastructure is financed may continue to shadow the stock.
importance:
• At this size, the listing is a landmark event for equity markets and AI investment alike.

• Its reception serves as a real-time referendum on investor conviction in the AI build-out.

• That it rose on a sharply down day highlights how selectively investors are still backing AI leaders.
